question: What does the Nabataean epitaph of Raqōš say?
answer: The Nabataean epitaph of Raqōš states that "Ka'b bar Haritat made for Raqash daughter of 'Abd-Manat, his mother" a grave, and that "she died in al-Hijr, year one-hundred-sixty-two, in the month of Tammuz." [S1] The inscription includes a curse: "may Mare 'Alma [the Lord of the World] curse him who alters this tomb or opens it, save for him whom he has begotten. And may he curse anyone who buries or exhumes anyone else in it." [S1]

english.text: As for this grave/This is a grave, which Ka'b bar Haritat made for Raqash daughter of 'Abd-Manat, his mother. And she died in al-Hijr, year one-hundred-sixty-two, in the month of Tammuz. And may Mare 'Alma [the Lord of the World] curse him who alters this tomb or opens it, save for him whom he has begotten. And may he curse anyone who buries or exhumes anyone else in it.
english.attribution: M. O'Connor's 1986 reading, as reproduced on Wikipedia (JSNab 17), building on Healey's editio.

english.text: §5 And about eight hundred stadia beyond there is another very deep bay, with a great mound of sand piled up at the right of the entrance; at the bottom of which the opsidian stone is found, and this is the only place where it is produced. These places, from the Calf-Eaters to the other Berber country, are governed by Zoskales, who is miserly in his ways and always striving for more, but otherwise upright, and acquainted with Greek literature.
english.attribution: Wilfred H. Schoff translation (1912), with emendations from Lionel Casson's 1989 Princeton edition, hosted by ToposText.

english.text: [§1] I, the Mazda-worshipping god Shapur, king of kings of Iran and Not-Iran, whose race is of the gods, son of the Mazda-worshipping god Ardashir, king of kings of Iran, whose race is of the gods, grandson of the god King Pabag, am lord of Iran. [§20] From the land of Thrace, from the land of Bithynia, from the land of Asia, from the land of Pamphylia, from the land of Isauria, from the land of Lyconia, from the land of Galatia, from the land of Lycia, from the land of Cilicia, from the land of Cappadocia, from the land of Phrygia, from the land of Syria.
english.attribution: Jake Nabel, Parthian Sources Online, translating the Parthian text of Huyse 1999.

english.text: §28 There are imported into this place from Egypt a little wheat and wine, as at Muza; clothing in the Arabian style, plain and common and most of it spurious; and copper and tin and coral and storax and other things such as go to Muza; and for the King usually wrought gold and silver plate, also horses, statuettes, and thin clothing of fine quality. And there are exported from this place, native produce, frankincense and aloes, and the rest of the things that enter into the trade of the other ports. The voyage to this place is best made at the same time as that to Muza, or rather earlier.
english.attribution: Wilfred H. Schoff translation (1912), as adapted/hosted by ToposText.

english.text: In the name of Allah, the Rahman — have mercy upon us, O lord of the heavens; satisfy us by means of your favor; and grant us the essence of it at the end/gift of our days.
english.attribution: Ahmad Al-Jallad, 'A pre-Islamic basmala: reflections on its first epigraphic attestation and its original significance', Jerusalem Studies in Arabic and Islam 52 (2022): 1–28.

english.text: Aeizanas, king of the Aksumites, Himyarites and Raeidan, the Ethiopians, the Sabaeans and Silei, Tiamo and the Beja and Kasu, king of kings, son of the invincible god Ares.
